body:
What are archaeological sources?

Archaeological sources are surviving material remains associated with past human activity. They include tools, pottery, houses, fortifications, drains, ornaments, seals, weights, burials and other objects or structures.

These remains are especially important for periods in which written evidence is unavailable or cannot be understood. They also supplement written records from later periods.

What different remains can reveal

  • Stone tools: evidence about cutting, scraping and other activities of early humans.
  • Pottery and storage vessels: evidence about storing, preparing and consuming food.
  • Seeds and animal bones: evidence about plants and animals used as food, although the interpretation must depend on the particular remains.
  • Buildings and drains: evidence about construction, settlement organisation and arrangements for water or wastewater.
  • Beads, ornaments and specialised tools: evidence about craft production and the use of different materials.
  • Seals and weights: evidence relevant to identifying objects, standardisation and possible exchange activities.

The evidence may support a conclusion without explaining every detail. For example, charred grains provide evidence that certain grains were present at a settlement, but they do not automatically establish every method by which those grains were cultivated.

The Harappan civilisation as an archaeological example

The Harappan civilisation, particularly its Mature phase of approximately 2600–1900 BCE, is known primarily through material remains. Archaeological evidence includes planned streets, houses, drains, seals, beads, pottery, weights and tools.

At Mohenjodaro, buildings, streets and drains reveal features of urban planning. Its Great Bath is a distinctive structure, although its precise use is not established beyond doubt.

Harappan seals contain signs that remain undeciphered. Consequently, archaeologists can describe many aspects of Harappan material life but cannot reliably read the names, orders or narratives that the signs may represent.

Dholavira: water management in Gujarat

Dholavira is located on Khadir Island in Kachchh, Gujarat. It was a major Harappan settlement with fortifications, streets, houses, water-storage structures and evidence of craft production.

The broader archaeological occupation at Dholavira extends approximately from 3000 to 1500 BCE. This does not mean that its entire period of occupation belongs to the Mature Harappan phase of 2600–1900 BCE.

Large reservoirs and other water-management structures are particularly important because the settlement occupied an arid region where water was scarce. These remains support the conclusion that inhabitants developed arrangements to collect and store water.

Lothal: crafts, trade and a large basin

Lothal, in present-day Gujarat near the Gulf of Khambhat, is another important Harappan site. Its remains include planned settlement areas, drains, evidence of bead-making, sealings and a large basin.

The basin is commonly interpreted as a dockyard, and the site is frequently associated with maritime exchange. However, the precise identification and function of the basin should be treated as an interpretation rather than an unquestionable fact.

Seals, sealings, craft remains and objects connected with distant regions help establish Lothal's importance in discussions of Harappan trade.

Other examples of archaeological evidence

SitePresent-day locationImportant evidence
BhimbetkaMadhya PradeshPrehistoric rock shelters and paintings
MohenjodaroPakistanUrban structures, drains and the Great Bath
KalibanganRajasthanEvidence of a ploughed field associated with Early Harappan levels
DholaviraGujaratFortifications, reservoirs and craft remains
LothalGujaratBead-making remains, sealings and a large basin

An archaeological discovery should not be made to answer questions beyond its evidence. The existence of a seal does not establish that its script has been deciphered. Similarly, finding an object at a site does not necessarily prove that it was manufactured there.

Prelims focus

  • Dholavira and Lothal are major Harappan sites in Gujarat.
  • Dholavira is on Khadir Island in Kachchh and is especially noted for water-management structures.
  • Lothal is associated with bead-making, sealings and a large basin commonly identified as a dockyard.
  • Kalibangan in Rajasthan provides evidence of a ploughed field.
  • Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh is associated with prehistoric rock shelters.
  • Trap: The Harappan script remains undeciphered despite the discovery of seals bearing signs.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 2, pp. 12–16; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, pp. 1–9; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Description and Brief Synthesis, consulted 17 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List 5918, Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal, Description, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Dholavira's water-storage structures are important evidence of Harappan urban planning.

title: Archaeological Sources and Major Sites in India and Gujarat

body:
What is an inscription?

An inscription is writing recorded on a material such as stone, metal, pottery or another durable surface. Ancient inscriptions were often engraved on rocks, pillars and copper plates.

Inscriptions may record royal orders, donations, land grants, achievements, religious messages or the construction and repair of public works. The study of inscriptions is called epigraphy.

Language and script are different

A language is a system used to communicate meaning through words. A script is the system of written signs used to represent language.

For example, an inscription may be written in the Prakrit language using the Brahmi script. Brahmi is therefore not another name for Prakrit.

TermMeaningHistorical example
LanguageThe language of the wordsPrakrit or Sanskrit
ScriptThe writing systemBrahmi or Kharosthi
InscriptionThe written record on a surfaceAn Ashokan rock edict

Ashokan inscriptions

Ashoka, a Mauryan ruler of the 3rd century BCE, had messages engraved on rocks and pillars. These inscriptions provide contemporary evidence about his policies and his conception of dhamma, which included moral conduct and respect for others.

Most Ashokan inscriptions are written in Prakrit using Brahmi script. Some inscriptions in the northwestern subcontinent use Kharosthi, while inscriptions associated with Afghanistan also include Greek and Aramaic.

The differences in language and script reflect the linguistic diversity of the regions in which the messages were recorded. It is incorrect to assume that every Ashokan inscription was written in Sanskrit.

James Prinsep and decipherment

Decipherment means establishing how an unfamiliar writing system can be read. In 1838, James Prinsep successfully deciphered Ashokan Brahmi after earlier investigations by several scholars.

In many inscriptions, Ashoka used titles such as Devanampiya and Piyadassi. Comparison with inscriptions that also named Ashoka helped establish the ruler's identity.

Girnar and Junagadh: inscriptions from different periods

The Girnar region near Junagadh in Gujarat is particularly important because inscriptions associated with different rulers and periods survive at the site.

Ashoka's rock edicts

The Girnar rock bears 14 major rock edicts of Ashoka, dating to approximately the 3rd century BCE. These are associated with the Mauryan ruler's public messages and are written in Brahmi script.

Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription

The inscription of Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman at Junagadh is dated to 150 CE, corresponding to Saka year 72. It is written in the Sanskrit language using Brahmi script.

The inscription records the restoration of Sudarshana Lake, which had suffered damage from flooding. It also recounts earlier work associated with the lake. According to the inscription, the lake was originally constructed under Chandragupta Maurya through his governor Pushyagupta, and improvements were undertaken during Ashoka's reign through Tushaspha.

Skandagupta's inscription

A later inscription associated with the Gupta ruler Skandagupta, from the 5th century CE, also records work connected with Sudarshana Lake.

These inscriptions are a useful example of how records at the same place can provide evidence of successive periods without belonging to the same dynasty or century.

Prashastis and copper-plate grants

A prashasti is a composition written in praise of a ruler or patron. It can record royal achievements, but its language may include exaggeration.

The Prayaga Prashasti, also called the Allahabad Pillar Inscription, was composed by Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta, a ruler of the 4th century CE. It is a significant source for Gupta political history, while its praise of the ruler must be recognised as the language of a courtly composition.

Copper-plate inscriptions frequently recorded grants of land or related rights. They are important evidence for political authority, donations and landholding arrangements, especially in early medieval India.

What inscriptions can and cannot establish

An inscription can establish that a particular message was engraved and may identify its issuer, language, place and date. It does not automatically prove that every royal claim was accurate or that every instruction was obeyed.

Damage, missing letters and changes in language can also limit interpretation. A claim about a completed public work is stronger when supported by surviving material remains or another relevant source.

Prelims focus

  • Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions; Brahmi and Kharosthi are scripts.
  • Most Ashokan inscriptions used Prakrit language and Brahmi script.
  • James Prinsep deciphered Ashokan Brahmi in 1838.
  • Girnar near Junagadh preserves Ashokan rock edicts of the 3rd century BCE.
  • Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription dates to 150 CE and uses Sanskrit language and Brahmi script.
  • Trap: Ashoka, Rudradaman and Skandagupta belong to different periods despite their inscriptions being associated with the same site.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, pp. 28–29, 32–33, 36–38 and 46–49; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 2, pp. 18–20; Archaeological Survey of India, Bharat SHRI, Photo Gallery, Brahmi Inscription of Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman from Junagadh, consulted 17 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, District Junagadh, Ashok Shilalekh, consulted 17 November 2026; Shubhra Pramanik, Significant Discoveries around Sudarshan Lake, Junagadh, Puratattva 35, 2004–05, pp. 179–180.]

title: Inscriptions: Languages, Scripts, Rulers and Gujarat Examples

body:
Why are coins important?

Coins are important historical sources because they can preserve symbols, inscriptions, portraits and evidence of exchange. The study of coins is known as numismatics.

Coins are material objects and may also contain inscriptions. Their value as evidence depends on their features and historical context.

What can a coin reveal?

  • Political information: the name or image of a ruler, a title or a symbol associated with authority.
  • Economic information: the use of coinage in exchange and monetary transactions.
  • Religious and cultural information: deities, symbols, motifs or legends represented on coins.
  • Connections between regions: coins found beyond their likely place of issue may provide evidence relevant to trade and movement.

The presence of a coin at a site does not automatically establish that the ruler who issued it governed that site. Coins can travel through trade, payment, gifts and later circulation.

Important coin traditions in ancient India

Punch-marked coins

Among the earliest coins used in the Indian subcontinent were punch-marked silver and copper coins, appearing from approximately the 6th century BCE.

They are called punch-marked because symbols were stamped or punched onto the metal. They are important evidence for the growth of monetary exchange in early historic India.

Indo-Greek coins

The Indo-Greeks, who ruled parts of the northwestern subcontinent from approximately the 2nd century BCE, issued some of the earliest Indian-region coins bearing the names and images of rulers.

Coins carrying legends in Greek and Kharosthi also contributed to the understanding of the Kharosthi script.

Kushana coins

The Kushanas issued important gold coins from approximately the 1st century CE. Their coins are useful for studying rulers, titles, religious imagery and monetary exchange.

Gupta coins

Gupta rulers issued notable gold coins, especially from the 4th century CE onwards. These coins are important sources for the representation of rulers and aspects of Gupta political and cultural history.

Roman coins and trade with India

Roman coins have been found at archaeological sites in southern India. These finds, together with other evidence, indicate commercial connections across the Indian Ocean.

They do not establish that southern India was part of the Roman Empire. The movement of coins through trade must be distinguished from the expansion of political control.

Limits of coin evidence

A ruler's name on a coin can help identify the issuing authority, but the coin alone may not establish the complete boundaries of the ruler's kingdom. Likewise, a large group of coins found at 1 site does not necessarily describe every aspect of the region's economy.

Coins are most informative when considered alongside inscriptions, archaeological remains and written records.

Prelims focus

  • Numismatics is the study of coins.
  • Silver and copper punch-marked coins were used from approximately the 6th century BCE.
  • Indo-Greek coins are notable for early ruler names and images.
  • Kushanas issued important gold coins from approximately the 1st century CE.
  • Gupta rulers issued notable gold coins from the 4th century CE onwards.
  • Trap: Roman coins found in India indicate connections through exchange; they do not prove Roman political rule over India.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, pp. 44–48.]

title: Coins as Sources of Political and Economic History
